newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: "Ramos is God's chosen," Manila marchers say.
newsitem.headline: "Ramos is God's chosen," Manila marchers say.

text.p: Die-hard supporters of Philippine President Fidel Ramos, demanding a second term for him, on Monday pressed on with their attempts to rewrite a constitution designed to keep away potential dictators.

Invoking God, about 1,000 Filipinos marched in central Manila with bundles of paper containing 5.5 million signatures to demand a plebiscite that would allow Ramos to run for re-election in next year's election.

"We believe that the chosen one of God will be our next leader...I think it's our President Ramos," evangelist Moreno Santander said as the Ramos loyalists marched to the Commission on Election (Comelec) to present their petition. The 10-year-old constitution, a reaction to late Ferdinand Marcos's harsh 20-year rule, limits a president to one term of six years. Leaders of the citizens' group P eople's Initiative for Reform, Modernisation and Action (PIRMA) launched the signature campaign to try to force a referendum to lift the term limits and permit Ramos to run for re-election when his present term expires in June 1998.

Ramos has said he will step down next year but some of his aides have said he deserves another shot at the presidency to continue his reform programme, which has lifted the country from bankruptcy to being one of Asia's most dynamic economies.
The Supreme Court on June 10 rejected PIRMA's petition for a plebiscite, but PIRMA said the issue was for the people to decide.

The election commission accepted the petition, accompanied by the signatures, and said it would meet soon to decide what to do with it. Poll officials earlier said they might just consign the papers to the archives in the face of the Supreme Court's ruling.
Roman Catholic Church leaders and opposition politicians aspiring to succeed Ramos have said the petition is a recipe for a Ramos dictatorship.

"There is no law to prevent any person from gathering signatures as there is no law preventing anyone from gathering garbage," scoffed opposition senator Miriam Santiago, an outspoken critic of efforts to change the constitution.
